what.text: Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring saturated dicarboxylic acid (1,7-heptanedicarboxylic acid, C9H16O4, molecular weight 188.22). It is part of the normal diet, in whole-grain cereals and animal products, and the body also makes small amounts of it.
How it acts, according to the FDA labels

items.text: The Azelex label says the exact mechanism is not known. In lab tests it is active against Propionibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis, two skin bacteria. The label says the clinical meaning of these lab findings is unknown.
Skin biopsies from people using Azelex showed a thinner outer skin layer and less filaggrin, a skin protein. The label says this suggests it may reduce the tiny blocked pores that start acne.
The Finacea label says the way it works in rosacea is unknown.
About 4% of azelaic acid put on the skin is absorbed into the body. Blood levels after use stay in the range people already have from diet.

research.text: The main human evidence for azelaic acid is the pair of 12-week randomized trials FDA reviewed for Finacea gel in rosacea, 664 people in total. Older European acne trials tested the 20% cream. No published trial of a cream that combines azelaic acid and niacinamide turned up in a PubMed search on October 31, 2026.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Finacea gel 15% in rosacea: two trials (FDA label)

facts.v: 2 multicenter, randomized, double-blind trials with identical protocols, comparing the gel with its gel base (vehicle)
664 adults with mild to moderate papulopustular rosacea (333 on Finacea, 331 on vehicle). 73% women, 92.5% white, mean age 49 (21 to 86)
change in the count of inflamed bumps (papules and pustules), and the investigator's global score

research.found: Inflamed bumps fell by an average 57.9% on Finacea vs 39.9% on vehicle in study one, and 50.0% vs 38.2% in study two. 61% vs 40%, and 61% vs 48%, were rated clear, minimal or mild at the end. The label says its effect on redness without bumps was not evaluated.

research.title: Azelaic acid 20% cream in acne (Katsambas et al.)

facts.v: one double-blind trial against the cream base (vehicle), and one single-blind trial against tretinoin 0.05% cream
92 people with moderate inflammatory acne (vehicle trial); 289 people with comedonal acne (tretinoin trial)
acne lesion counts and overall response

research.found: The authors report the 20% cream reduced lesion counts more than its vehicle, and matched tretinoin for blackheads and whiteheads with fewer local side effects. Only the abstract was reviewed for this page.

src.label: Katsambas et al., Acta Derm Venereol Suppl, 1989

items.text: In a 26-week study in genetically modified (Tg.AC) mice, twice-daily Finacea gel and the gel base alone both raised the number of male mice with skin papillomas at the treated site. The label says the effect may come from the gel base and that its relevance to people is not clear.
At high oral doses that also harmed the mothers, azelaic acid was toxic to embryos in rats, rabbits and monkeys. No birth defects were seen. It did not damage DNA in lab tests.

us.text: Azelaic acid is FDA approved, by prescription, in Azelex 20% cream for acne (1995) and Finacea 15% gel (2002) and foam (2015) for rosacea. Compounded versions, including combinations with other ingredients, are not FDA approved. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: approved September 13, 1995 (NDA 020428) for mild to moderate inflammatory acne vulgaris.
approved December 24, 2002 (NDA 021470) for the inflamed papules and pustules of mild to moderate rosacea.
approved July 29, 2015 (NDA 207071) for the same rosacea use.
FDA has also approved generic azelaic acid gels from several makers.

world.lead: Azelaic acid is an approved prescription skin medicine in the US and is authorised as a medicine across most of the EU and in Northern Ireland. Canada and Australia could not be checked. It is not on the WADA Prohibited List.

after.text: Azelaic acid is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, in any class, in or out of competition.

side.text: The FDA labels list mostly skin reactions where it is applied: burning, stinging, itching and dryness, usually in the first weeks. They also report lightening of the skin in some people and rare flares of asthma and cold sores.

items.text: among 457 people on the gel, the most common skin reactions were burning, stinging or tingling, then itching, scaling or dry skin, and redness or irritation. In a 15-week study, treatment-related skin reactions occurred in 19.4% on Finacea and 7.1% on the comparison gel.
itching, burning, stinging and tingling in about 1 to 5% of patients. Redness, dryness, rash, peeling, irritation and dermatitis in under 1%.
there have been isolated reports of hypopigmentation (lighter skin). Both labels say azelaic acid has not been well studied in people with dark skin, who should be watched for early signs.
worsening of asthma, vitiligo-like loss of skin colour, small pale spots, extra hair growth, reddening around hair follicles and flare-ups of cold sores (herpes labialis).
inflammation inside the eye (iridocyclitis) has been reported after Finacea gel got into the eye by accident.
there are no adequate studies in pregnant women. High oral doses harmed embryos in animal studies.
Finacea gel must not be used by people allergic to propylene glycol or any other ingredient.

side.text: These are the reactions recorded for FDA-approved azelaic acid products. Compounded creams that combine azelaic acid with other ingredients have not been tested in trials of their own.

surprises: Azelaic acid is often sold as a redness treatment, but the Finacea label says its effect on rosacea redness without bumps has not been evaluated; it is approved only for the inflamed bumps.

Azelaic acid is often promoted to even out or brighten skin tone, while both FDA labels warn of isolated reports of skin lightening (hypopigmentation) and say it has not been well studied in dark skin.
